CASE OF THE MONTH
Section Editors
Robert C. Griggs, MD
Rochester, New York
Jerry R. Mendell, MD
Columbus, Ohio
Robert G. Miller, MD
San Francisco, California
ABSTRACT: We report the first case of stiff-persons’ (-man) syndrome in
the setting of a histologically proven thymoma. Muscular hyperactivity
was abolished under general anesthesia and the symptoms of stiffness
resolved after thymectomy and three courses of intravenous immunoglob-
ulins. After thymectomy, the patient developed ocular myasthenia gravis
which later resolved spontaneously. We suggest that thymoma be sought
for in cases with neuromuscular hyperactivity syndromes. Myasthenia
gravis may develop subsequently in these cases.

Key words: stiff-man syndrome; Isaacs’ syndrome; intravenous immuno-
globulin G; thymoma; myasthenia gravis
STIFF-PERSONS’ SYNDROME
ASSOCIATED WITH THYMOMA AND
SUBSEQUENT MYASTHENIA GRAVIS
ANTHONY P. NICHOLAS, MD, PhD,1 ANJAN CHATTERJEE, MD,1
MUOI M. ARNOLD, MD,2 GWENDOLYN C. CLAUSSEN, MD,1
GEORGE L. ZORN, Jr, MD,3 and SHIN J. OH, MD1*
1 Department of Neurology, University of Alabama at Birmingham, U.A.B. Station,
Birmingham, Alabama 35294-0007, USA
2 Department of Pathology, University of Alabama at Birmingham,
Birmingham, Alabama, USA
3 Department of Surgery, University of Alabama at Birmingham,
Birmingham, Alabama, USA
Received 24 May 1996; accepted 7 September 1996
Neuromuscular hyperactivity syndromes, including
stiff-persons’ syndrome (SPS) and neuromyotonia or
Isaacs’ syndrome, are rare neurological disorders
which present with continuous, involuntary muscu-
lar activity. SPS, first described in 1956 by Moersch
and Woltman,
30 is characterized by persistent, pain-
ful axial and proximal limb muscle rigidity and
spasms exacerbated by sensory or motor stimuli and
abolished by sleep or general anesthesia.
8 The
syndrome may be associated with diabetes 41–43 and
epilepsy.43 The underlying pathophysiology of the
disorder remains obscure; however, autoimmune
mechanisms are implicated. Two thirds of patients
with SPS demonstrate circulating antibodies re-
active to glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), sug-
gesting an impairment of gamma-aminobutyric
acid (GABA)ergic neurotransmission.
16 Other or-
gan-specific antibodies have also been reported
in SPS.
6,7,9,13,16,41–43,47 Recently it has been rec-
ognized that SPS may occur as a paraneoplastic syn-
drome.1,5,12,13,16,24,34,35,38,46 Neuromyotonia is also
characterized by clinical symptoms of stiffness and
continuous muscular activity.
20,28,32 Spasms and
twitching clinically resembling fasciculations or myo-
kymia may be present. Unlike SPS, general anesthe-
sia or nerve blocks do not abolish the muscular
activity; however, curare does. An autoimmune etiol-
ogy has also been proposed for neuromyotonia,
where it has been suggested that the pathology in
this condition is caused by antibodies against potas-
sium channels in neuronal membranes near or at
the neuromuscular junction.
32,40
There has been 1 reported case with SPS, myas-
thenia gravis (MG), and a mediastinal mass, which
was suspected to be a thymoma, but the pathology of
the mass was not verified.
34,35 To our knowledge, the
following is the first documented case of a patient
with SPS, MG, and histologically proven thymoma
containing active germinal centers.
CASE REPORT
A 55-year-old man began to experience cramping
pains in his legs in August, 1993. Since he worked as

a roofer, he was initially treated with four courses of

antitetanus toxoid immune globulin with no relief of
symptoms. By November of 1993, his painful muscle
contractions and spasms had worsened, involving
limb (legs > arms) and axial muscles, the latter pro-
ducing hyperlordosis. Neurological examination re-
vealed a well-developed, well-nourished, middle-
aged man who was alert and oriented. He had
diffuse hyperhydrosis. Mental status was normal. Cra-
nial nerve examination was normal except for a vi-
sual acuity of 20/40 bilaterally. He had no nystagmus
or involuntary tongue or facial muscle movements.
Trismus or risus sardonicus were not present. Motor
exam showed normal bulk and strength in all muscle
groups. He had diffuse axial and lower limb stiffness
without spasticity or cogwheeling. His toes remained
fixed in extension and he experienced pain when
flexion of his ankles was attempted. Clinical myoky-
mia was present in the gastrocnemius muscles. Sen-
sory examination was normal. Reflexes were brisk
but symmetric throughout, and plantar responses
were equivocal bilaterally. His coordination was con-
sistent with his stiffness. Gait was wide-based. He had
difficulty lifting his legs off the floor due to move-
ment-induced spasms. With the slightest tapping to
elicit a jaw jerk reflex, he had painful extensor
spasms of his entire body assuming an opistotonic
posture. It also was difficult for him to take medica-
tions, since even bringing his hand to his mouth
elicited this response. Auditory, emotional, and tac-
tile stimuli also produced similar painful spasms.
He had normal complete blood counts, electro-
lytes, liver enzymes, vitamin B12 level, thyroid func-
tion, and coagulation studies. Human T-cell lympho-
tropic virus, type 1 antibodies and tuberculin
purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test were
negative. C-reactive protein was 0.7 mg/dL. Anti-
nuclear antibodies were present at a titer of 1:40 and
demonstrated a nucleolar pattern. Serum protein
immunoelectrophoresis also showed no monoclonal
antibodies. Antimyelin associated glycoprotein, anti-
GM1, anti-GAD, antiacetylcholine receptor, and anti-
Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibodies were not de-
tected. Electroencephalogram was normal. Magnetic
resonance imaging and angiography of the brain
and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. Lumbar
puncture had an opening pressure of 120 mm. Ce-
rebrospinal fluid analysis showed no white blood
cells, a protein of 54 mg/dL, glucose of 72 mg/dL,
no growth on cultures, and a normal immunoglob-
ulin G (IgG) index without oligoclonal bands.
Motor, sensory, and mixed nerve conductions
were normal. There were no repetitive discharges in
the compound muscle action potentials in the motor
nerve conduction studies, nor were afterdischarges
seen following the M, H, or F waves. Motor neuron
hyperexcitability was documented by high H-reflex
to M-wave amplitude ratios of 0.38–0.62 (normal <
0.38),
3 an F-wave to M-wave amplitude ratio of 0.15
(normal <0.05),10 T-reflex amplitudes of 9–19 mV in
the ankle (normal <8.8 mV), 21 and T-reflex ampli-
tudes of 8.5–16 mV in the patella (normal <3.9
mV).
21 An absent silent period was observed in mas-
seter reflex testing. Needle electromyography
showed continuous motor unit potentials (MUPs) in
numerous leg muscles, some of which increased with
effort and tapping of muscle. The continuous MUPs
at rest in the gastrocnemius muscle were abolished
under general anesthesia (Fig. 1). No myokymic dis-
charges, neuromyotonic discharges, or double,

triple, or multiple bursts of MUPs were seen with
electromyographic testing.

strated a mediastinal mass that was subsequently di-
agnosed as thymoma by needle biopsy. The patient
was treated with diazepam 40 mg/day and baclofen
80 mg/day in divided doses. Despite some improve-
ment in his stiffness, he continued to have difficulty
getting to the bathroom from his bed in the hospital
room. In January, 1994, the patient received a 5-day
course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) without
noticeable benefit. One day after the last dose of
intravenous IgG, the patient had a thymectomy,
which was followed by clinical improvement.
The surgical specimen (Fig. 2A) consisted of a
7.0 × 5.0 × 3.0 cm encapsulated mass with soft grey
cut surfaces and central dystrophic calcification. Mi-
croscopically, the tumor was a cortical thymoma with
lobules of large, oval, cytokeratin-positive cells ad-
mixed with moderate number of lymphocytes and
rare areas of medullary differentiation without Has-
sall’s corpuscles. Lymphoid follicles with prominent
germinal centers were present within the tumor and
in the remaining atrophic thymic tissues, which were
positive for B-cell markers (Fig. 2B).
Approximately 2 months after thymectomy, the
patient complained of diplopia. Examination
showed weakness in the right lateral rectus and left
medial rectus muscles. A Tensilon test at that time
was negative. His eye movement abnormalities per-
sisted and 2 weeks later he developed right facial
weakness. Rapid nerve stimulation of the flexor carpi
ulnaris, adductor digiti quinti, trapezius, and obicu-
laris occuli were all normal. Single-fiber electromy-
ography on the extensor digitorum communis was
normal, with a mean consecutive difference of 13
single-fiber potential pairs of 21 µs (normal <40.4
µs).
39 However, single-fiber electromyography on
the frontalis muscle showed abnormal jitter, with a
mean consecutive difference of 17 single-fiber po-
tential pairs of 33 µs (normal <30 µs)
39 and two
single-fiber potential pairs longer than 45 µs, which
is consistent with ocular myasthenia gravis.
39 Prostig-
mine injection of 1.5 mg given intramuscularly re-
sulted in marked improvement of extraocular eye
movements. He was temporarily maintained on pyr-
idostigmine alone (60 mg q.i.d. and one Timespan
180 mg q.h.s.), but within 12 months was tapered off
this and is presently asymptomatic for myasthenia
gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies remain un-
detectable.
Fourteen months after thymectomy, painful
muscle spasms returned and were only moderately
controlled by diazepam and baclofen. Again, a 5-day
course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) was ad-
ministered and this produced marked clinical im-
provement. Twenty-nine months after thymectomy,
the patient again had a recurrence of symptoms. At
that time, a 3-day course of intravenous IgG (400
mg/kg/day) was administered, which produced
marked clinical improvement. The patient is pres-
ently well controlled on diazepam (10 mg three
times daily) and baclofen (10 mg three times daily).
He ambulates by himself without any stiffness of his
legs or trunk.
DISCUSSION
We report the first documented case of SPS asso-
ciated with histologically proven thymoma. After
thymectomy, the patient later developed ocular my-
asthenia, which later resolved spontaneously. Thy-
moma was of the cortical type and frequent lym-
phoid follicles with prominent germinal centers
were seen within the tumor and in the remaining
thymic tissues, features highly associated with
MG.

To our knowledge, 8 other cases of neuromuscu-
lar hyperactivity syndromes associated with thymoma
have been reported (Table 1). Piccolo and cowork-
ers reported a man with onset of symptoms of SPS at
the age of 54 with radiographic evidence of a medi-
astinal tumor, presumed to be a thymoma.
34,35
When his symptoms of stiffness and cramping spon-
taneously resolved after 6 years, he developed gen-
eralized myasthenia gravis. He also had elevated ace-
tylcholine receptor antibodies. The presence of
thymoma was not histologically verified in that case.
The other 7 cases of neuromuscular hyperactivity
associated with underlying thymoma
14,18,22,25,33 were
compatible with the diagnosis of neuromyoto-
nia.
20,28,32
In previous case reports, the combination of neu-
romyotonia and thymoma has been associated with
encephalopathic features,
18,25 or signs of peripheral
neuropathy.14 It has been shown (Table 1) that these
patients often had elevated acetylcholine receptor
antibodies with or without symptoms of myasthenia
gravis.
14,18,33 Also, MG may develop before 14,33 or
after thymectomy in these cases. 14,25 Seven of the 8
(perhaps all) cases of reported neuromyotonia and
suspected thymoma actually had mixed features of
SPS and neuromyotonia (Table 1). Our patient also
had some atypical features for SPS, such as clinical
myokymia, brisk reflexes, equivocal plantar re-
sponses, and hyperhydrosis.
It has been argued that one can differentiate SPS
from neuromyotonia by clinical features (Table 2),
although overlap in clinical symptomatology be-
tween these two disorders has been noted.
15,23,45
Classically, neuromyotonia symptoms usually re-
spond to antiepileptics such as phenytoin or car-
bamazepine,
20,28 while SPS usually responds to
GABAergic medications such as diazepam, 19 baclo-
fen,29,49 and valproate, 44 or alpha-2 adrenergic re-
ceptor agonists such as clonidine. 26,27 Also in SPS,
muscular hyperactivity has been shown to subside
during stage 3 and REM sleep. 17
In our opinion, the abolition of muscular hyper-
activity under general anesthesia confirmed the di-
agnosis of SPS in this case, and certainly ruled out
the possibility of neuromyotonia. Furthermore, typi-
cal neurophysiological findings sometimes seen in
neuromyotonia but not in SPS (see Ref. 4 for re-
view), such as repetitive discharges after the H, F, or

M waves in nerve conduction studies or myokymic
discharges, neuromyotonic discharges, and double,
triple, or multiple bursts of MUPs in electromyogra-
phy, were not present in our case.
Since no anti-GAD antibodies were seen in our
case, and since abolition of muscular hyperactivity
with general anesthesia can also be seen in voluntary
muscular hyperactivity and tetanus, these diagnoses
were briefly entertained. However, in this patient,
continuous, involuntary MUP discharges in the gas-
trocnemius were documented at rest, which actually
resembled myokymia clinically. It was these dis-
charges that were abolished under general anesthe-
sia (Fig. 1). This observation, accompanied by the
patient’s predictable recurrence of symptoms (on av-
erage every 14 months) and favorable response to
intravenous IgG on those occasions, suggested that
the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than that of
voluntary muscular overactivity. Similar to tetanus,
the silent period in masseter muscle testing in this
case was absent; however, the lack of history of a
wound or trauma, the duration and persistence of
symptoms after being treated with antitetanus im-
mune globulin, and the lack of other common signs
of tetanus such as trismus and risus sardonicus sug-
gested that the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than
that of ‘‘chronic’’ tetanus.
37
Plasmapheresis has been efficacious in SPS asso-
ciated with anti-GAD antibodies, 6,47 but the efficacy
of plasmapheresis in the treatment of cases without
evidence of antineuronal antibodies is not known.
Recently, SPS symptoms have been reported to im-
prove with intravenous IgG.
2 In Picollo’s case, SPS
symptoms resolved spontaneously after 6 years. In
our SPS case, stiffness resolved after a combination
of one course of intravenous IgG and thymectomy,
only to return later at 14 and 29 months after thy-
mectomy, but then responded to subsequent courses
of intravenous IgG. Also in our case, myasthenic
symptoms developed after thymectomy, but there
were no detectable acetylcholine receptor antibod-
ies. One year after thymectomy, myasthenic symp-
toms resolved spontaneously in this patient.
We suggest that neuromuscular hyperactivity syn-
dromes may be paraneoplastic in the setting of thy-
moma. If a thymoma is uncovered, we suggest that
thymectomy be considered. Myasthenic symptoms
may develop before or after thymectomy in these
cases.

segments.text:
ABSTRACT: We report the first case of stiff-persons’ (-man) syndrome in
the setting of a histologically proven thymoma. Muscular hyperactivity
was abolished under general anesthesia and the symptoms of stiffness
resolved after thymectomy and three courses of intravenous immunoglob-
ulins. After thymectomy, the patient developed ocular myasthenia gravis
which later resolved spontaneously. We suggest that thymoma be sought
for in cases with neuromuscular hyperactivity syndromes. Myasthenia
gravis may develop subsequently in these cases.

CASE REPORT
A 55-year-old man began to experience cramping
pains in his legs in August, 1993. Since he worked as
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text: a roofer, he was initially treated with four courses of
segments.evidence: Deterministic clinical-window selection for Stage 07 single-case v1.

segments.text:
antitetanus toxoid immune globulin with no relief of
symptoms. By November of 1993, his painful muscle
contractions and spasms had worsened, involving
limb (legs > arms) and axial muscles, the latter pro-
ducing hyperlordosis. Neurological examination re-
vealed a well-developed, well-nourished, middle-
aged man who was alert and oriented. He had
diffuse hyperhydrosis. Mental status was normal. Cra-
nial nerve examination was normal except for a vi-
sual acuity of 20/40 bilaterally. He had no nystagmus
or involuntary tongue or facial muscle movements.
Trismus or risus sardonicus were not present. Motor
exam showed normal bulk and strength in all muscle
groups. He had diffuse axial and lower limb stiffness
without spasticity or cogwheeling. His toes remained
fixed in extension and he experienced pain when
flexion of his ankles was attempted. Clinical myoky-
mia was present in the gastrocnemius muscles. Sen-
sory examination was normal. Reflexes were brisk
but symmetric throughout, and plantar responses
were equivocal bilaterally. His coordination was con-
sistent with his stiffness. Gait was wide-based. He had
difficulty lifting his legs off the floor due to move-
ment-induced spasms. With the slightest tapping to
elicit a jaw jerk reflex, he had painful extensor
spasms of his entire body assuming an opistotonic
posture. It also was difficult for him to take medica-
tions, since even bringing his hand to his mouth
elicited this response. Auditory, emotional, and tac-
tile stimuli also produced similar painful spasms.
He had normal complete blood counts, electro-
lytes, liver enzymes, vitamin B12 level, thyroid func-
tion, and coagulation studies. Human T-cell lympho-
tropic virus, type 1 antibodies and tuberculin
purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test were
negative. C-reactive protein was 0.7 mg/dL. Anti-
nuclear antibodies were present at a titer of 1:40 and
demonstrated a nucleolar pattern. Serum protein
immunoelectrophoresis also showed no monoclonal
antibodies. Antimyelin associated glycoprotein, anti-
GM1, anti-GAD, antiacetylcholine receptor, and anti-
Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibodies were not de-
tected. Electroencephalogram was normal. Magnetic
resonance imaging and angiography of the brain
and spinal cord showed no abnormalities. Lumbar
puncture had an opening pressure of 120 mm. Ce-
rebrospinal fluid analysis showed no white blood
cells, a protein of 54 mg/dL, glucose of 72 mg/dL,
no growth on cultures, and a normal immunoglob-
ulin G (IgG) index without oligoclonal bands.
Motor, sensory, and mixed nerve conductions
were normal. There were no repetitive discharges in
the compound muscle action potentials in the motor
nerve conduction studies, nor were afterdischarges
seen following the M, H, or F waves. Motor neuron
hyperexcitability was documented by high H-reflex
to M-wave amplitude ratios of 0.38–0.62 (normal <
0.38),
3 an F-wave to M-wave amplitude ratio of 0.15
(normal <0.05),10 T-reflex amplitudes of 9–19 mV in
the ankle (normal <8.8 mV), 21 and T-reflex ampli-
tudes of 8.5–16 mV in the patella (normal <3.9
mV).
21 An absent silent period was observed in mas-
seter reflex testing. Needle electromyography
showed continuous motor unit potentials (MUPs) in
numerous leg muscles, some of which increased with
effort and tapping of muscle. The continuous MUPs
at rest in the gastrocnemius muscle were abolished
under general anesthesia (Fig. 1). No myokymic dis-
charges, neuromyotonic discharges, or double,

segments.text:
triple, or multiple bursts of MUPs were seen with
electromyographic testing.
Computer tomography of the chest demon-

neous MUPs at rest during general anesthesia.

segments.text:
strated a mediastinal mass that was subsequently di-
agnosed as thymoma by needle biopsy. The patient
was treated with diazepam 40 mg/day and baclofen
80 mg/day in divided doses. Despite some improve-
ment in his stiffness, he continued to have difficulty
getting to the bathroom from his bed in the hospital
room. In January, 1994, the patient received a 5-day
course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) without
noticeable benefit. One day after the last dose of
intravenous IgG, the patient had a thymectomy,
which was followed by clinical improvement.
The surgical specimen (Fig. 2A) consisted of a
7.0 × 5.0 × 3.0 cm encapsulated mass with soft grey
cut surfaces and central dystrophic calcification. Mi-
croscopically, the tumor was a cortical thymoma with
lobules of large, oval, cytokeratin-positive cells ad-
mixed with moderate number of lymphocytes and
rare areas of medullary differentiation without Has-
sall’s corpuscles. Lymphoid follicles with prominent
germinal centers were present within the tumor and
in the remaining atrophic thymic tissues, which were
positive for B-cell markers (Fig. 2B).
Approximately 2 months after thymectomy, the
patient complained of diplopia. Examination
showed weakness in the right lateral rectus and left
medial rectus muscles. A Tensilon test at that time
was negative. His eye movement abnormalities per-
sisted and 2 weeks later he developed right facial
weakness. Rapid nerve stimulation of the flexor carpi
ulnaris, adductor digiti quinti, trapezius, and obicu-
laris occuli were all normal. Single-fiber electromy-
ography on the extensor digitorum communis was
normal, with a mean consecutive difference of 13
single-fiber potential pairs of 21 µs (normal <40.4
µs).
39 However, single-fiber electromyography on
the frontalis muscle showed abnormal jitter, with a
mean consecutive difference of 17 single-fiber po-
tential pairs of 33 µs (normal <30 µs)
39 and two
single-fiber potential pairs longer than 45 µs, which
is consistent with ocular myasthenia gravis.
39 Prostig-
mine injection of 1.5 mg given intramuscularly re-
sulted in marked improvement of extraocular eye
movements. He was temporarily maintained on pyr-
idostigmine alone (60 mg q.i.d. and one Timespan
180 mg q.h.s.), but within 12 months was tapered off
this and is presently asymptomatic for myasthenia
gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibodies remain un-
detectable.
Fourteen months after thymectomy, painful
muscle spasms returned and were only moderately
controlled by diazepam and baclofen. Again, a 5-day
course of intravenous IgG (400 mg/kg/day) was ad-
ministered and this produced marked clinical im-
provement. Twenty-nine months after thymectomy,
the patient again had a recurrence of symptoms. At
that time, a 3-day course of intravenous IgG (400
mg/kg/day) was administered, which produced
marked clinical improvement. The patient is pres-
ently well controlled on diazepam (10 mg three
times daily) and baclofen (10 mg three times daily).
He ambulates by himself without any stiffness of his
legs or trunk.

segments.text:
Our patient also
had some atypical features for SPS, such as clinical
myokymia, brisk reflexes, equivocal plantar re-
sponses, and hyperhydrosis.
It has been argued that one can differentiate SPS
from neuromyotonia by clinical features (Table 2),
although overlap in clinical symptomatology be-
tween these two disorders has been noted.
15,23,45
Classically, neuromyotonia symptoms usually re-
spond to antiepileptics such as phenytoin or car-
bamazepine,
20,28 while SPS usually responds to
GABAergic medications such as diazepam, 19 baclo-
fen,29,49 and valproate, 44 or alpha-2 adrenergic re-
ceptor agonists such as clonidine. 26,27 Also in SPS,
muscular hyperactivity has been shown to subside
during stage 3 and REM sleep. 17
In our opinion, the abolition of muscular hyper-
activity under general anesthesia confirmed the di-
agnosis of SPS in this case, and certainly ruled out
the possibility of neuromyotonia. Furthermore, typi-
cal neurophysiological findings sometimes seen in
neuromyotonia but not in SPS (see Ref. 4 for re-
view), such as repetitive discharges after the H, F, or

segments.text:
M waves in nerve conduction studies or myokymic
discharges, neuromyotonic discharges, and double,
triple, or multiple bursts of MUPs in electromyogra-
phy, were not present in our case.
Since no anti-GAD antibodies were seen in our
case, and since abolition of muscular hyperactivity
with general anesthesia can also be seen in voluntary
muscular hyperactivity and tetanus, these diagnoses
were briefly entertained. However, in this patient,
continuous, involuntary MUP discharges in the gas-
trocnemius were documented at rest, which actually
resembled myokymia clinically. It was these dis-
charges that were abolished under general anesthe-
sia (Fig. 1). This observation, accompanied by the
patient’s predictable recurrence of symptoms (on av-
erage every 14 months) and favorable response to
intravenous IgG on those occasions, suggested that
the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than that of
voluntary muscular overactivity. Similar to tetanus,
the silent period in masseter muscle testing in this
case was absent; however, the lack of history of a
wound or trauma, the duration and persistence of
symptoms after being treated with antitetanus im-
mune globulin, and the lack of other common signs
of tetanus such as trismus and risus sardonicus sug-
gested that the diagnosis of SPS was more likely than
that of ‘‘chronic’’ tetanus.
37
Plasmapheresis has been efficacious in SPS asso-
ciated with anti-GAD antibodies, 6,47 but the efficacy
of plasmapheresis in the treatment of cases without
evidence of antineuronal antibodies is not known.
Recently, SPS symptoms have been reported to im-
prove with intravenous IgG.
2 In Picollo’s case, SPS
symptoms resolved spontaneously after 6 years. In
our SPS case, stiffness resolved after a combination
of one course of intravenous IgG and thymectomy,
only to return later at 14 and 29 months after thy-
mectomy, but then responded to subsequent courses
of intravenous IgG. Also in our case, myasthenic
symptoms developed after thymectomy, but there
were no detectable acetylcholine receptor antibod-
ies. One year after thymectomy, myasthenic symp-
toms resolved spontaneously in this patient.
We suggest that neuromuscular hyperactivity syn-
dromes may be paraneoplastic in the setting of thy-
moma. If a thymoma is uncovered, we suggest that
thymectomy be considered. Myasthenic symptoms
may develop before or after thymectomy in these
cases.
